results.title: Comparison and Application of Time-Frequency Analysis Methods for Nonstationary Signal Processing | Springer Nature Link
results.content: Communications in Computer and Information Science ((CCIS,volume 175)). Most of signals in engineering are nonstationary and time-varying. The Fourier transform as a traditional approach can only provide the feature information in frequency domain. The time-frequency techniques may give a comprehensive description of signals in time-frequency planes. Based on some typical nonstationary signals, five time-frequency analysis methods, i.e., the short-time Fourier transform (STFT), wavelet transform (WT), Wigner- Ville distribution (WVD), pseudo-WVD (PWVD) and the Hilbert-Huang transform (HHT), were performed and compared in this paper. Compared with the other methods, the HHT with a high time-frequency resolution can clearly describe the rules of the frequency compositions changing with time, is a good approach for feature extraction in nonstationary signal processing. results.title: Mastering Nonstationary Time Series Analysis: Methods and Techniques
results.content: # Mastering Nonstationary Time Series Analysis: Methods and Techniques. Nonstationary time series are a fundamental concept in the realm of data analysis, playing a crucial role in numerous fields such as economics, finance, and environmental science. Unlike stationary time series, nonstationary time series exhibit certain dynamic characteristics that change over time. A time series is deemed nonstationary when its statistical properties, such as mean, variance, and autocorrelation, change over time. Structural breaks are abrupt shifts in the data, caused by events such as policy changes or economic crises. Understanding these key characteristics is essential for accurate time series analysis. By understanding and correctly identifying the nonstationary elements in a time series, analysts can apply suitable methods, such as differencing, transformation, or advanced modeling techniques like ARIMA and GARCH, to mitigate these challenges. ## Understanding Trends in Time Series Data. Identifying and understanding these trends is crucial for analyzing nonstationary time series data, as they can significantly influence the forecasting and modeling processes.

results.title: Adaptive Bayesian Spectral Analysis of High-dimensional Nonstationary Time Series - PMC
results.content: The procedure is based on a novel frequency-domain factor model that provides a flexible yet parsimonious representation of spectral matrices from a large number of simultaneously observed time series. **Keywords:** Factor Analysis, High-dimensional Time Series, Locally Stationary Process, Multiplicative Gamma Process, Penalized Splines, Spectral Analysis, Stochastic Approximation Monte Carlo. These methods can be roughly grouped into three categories: methods that assume, in a manner similar to the rolling window estimator, power spectra evolve smoothly over time (Dahlhaus, 2000; Guo and Dai, 2006; Sanderson et al., 2010; Park et al., 2014), methods that are based on data-driven piecewise stationary approximations (Ombao et al., 2005; Davis et al., 2006), and adaptive Bayesian methods that can approximate both abrupt and slowly varying dynamics (Zhang, 2016; Li and Krafty, 2019). The primary contribution of this article is introducing an adaptive method for the spectral analysis of high-dimensional time series that can capture both abrupt and slowly varying dynamics efficiently while nonparmetricaly modeling spectral matrices. In this article, we present an adaptive nonparametric method for the spectral analysis of high-dimensional nonstationary time series. Section 2 presents the proposed frequency-domain factor model for high-dimensional nonstationary time series. This article considers *P*-dimensional vector-valued time series ***X****t* = (*X*1*t*, ⋯, *X**Pt*)′ that can be represented through a novel locally stationary factor model. Under this approach, a time series is adaptively partitioned into a random number of approximately stationary segments, local spectra are estimated within each segment, and time-varying power spectrum is obtained by averaging local estimates over the distribution of partitions. As described in Section 2, for the spectral analysis of a nonstationary time series, we adaptively estimate the unknown number and locations of the partition points. results.title: Personality traits, panel tenure, survey topic, and context as predictors of survey nonresponse patterns in high-frequency online longitudinal surveys - PMC
results.content: In this study, we analyze the independent effects of non-demographic variables—respondent personality traits, panel tenure, and survey topics, using unique datasets from two recently completed high-frequency online longitudinal studies conducted in the U.S. We used latent class analysis to group respondents into various classes based on similarities in their nonresponse patterns across all survey waves, which revealed substantial variations in patterns of nonresponse. In this study, we analyze the independent effects of non-demographic variables – respondent personality traits, panel tenure, and survey topics and context – that are likely to be important for predicting nonresponse patterns in high-frequency online longitudinal studies, as detailed below. Based on this expectation, we hypothesize that personality traits are important predictors of a respondent’s likelihood to participate consistently in online panel surveys and may have more explanatory power than conventional demographic and household variables commonly found in offline panel studies. While these studies rely on cross-sectional or dual-mode data, our study extends this work by using a richer 44-item personality battery and panel data to examine how personality traits predict actual nonresponse patterns over time in high-frequency online longitudinal surveys. Additionally, for sensitivity analysis and completeness, we provide in S1, S2, S3, and S4 Figs in the Supporting Information Section showing observed attrition patterns and in S3, S4, S5, S6 Tables in the Supporting Information Section presenting average marginal effects from multinomial logistic regression results predicting class membership: for the latent class models that are one class smaller and one class larger than the chosen number of latent classes for each of the two study samples, leading to similar substantive conclusions. Although the estimated average marginal effects of conscientiousness are negative in the regression models predicting membership in the “Non-respondents”, “Wave 10 Attritors”, “Mid-wave attritors” and “Good Responders” attrition classes in the monthly events study, they are not statistically significant after applying adjustments for multiple hypotheses tests.
